extracted.intended_audience: scholars, students, and translators of classical poetics and Aristotle / literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and critical principles for understanding and producing poetic imitation (mimesis) per Aristotle: how to conceive poetry, tragedy, diction, and translation choices in light of Aristotelian terminology and esoteric style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as μέμησις τὸ σύνολον (imitation of the whole)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is μέμησις τὸ σύνολον — literally 'imitation of the whole' (synolon = form + matter); rendered here as 'immaterial portrayal of the imaginary.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat poetry as creative art that imitates both form and matter (an 'immaterial portrayal'), not merely a copy of facts; the poet creates an ideal model (παράδειγμα) rather than a mere likeness (εἰκών).

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative vs. reproductive art (mimesis vs. ἀπεικάζειν)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish creative poetry (μέμησις) which 'portrays the imaginary' from reproductive art (ἀπεικασία) which copies form or appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creative works should invent or idealize (algebraic formula for qualities), whereas reproductive arts focus on likeness; in practice, poets may use familiar names but need not reproduce historical fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry should be imaginary, not mere history
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry 'must not be a reproduction of the actual history; it must be imaginary' and stands to history 'in the relation of algebra to tradesmen’s books.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing narrative/poetry, prefer constructed, unified fictional patterns that highlight essence and intelligibility over slavish factual reproduction; invention can exploit audience familiarity but is not bound by it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the 'ideal model' (παράδειγμα) in poetic creation
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet’s product can be a 'coin of fiction' — an ideal model that 'pretend[s] in every respect' and 'touches reality nowhere.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ coherent, internally plausible models and characters that function as paradigms rather than literal historical portraits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy: σπουδαῖος rendered 'heroic' — choice of tragic subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle gives σπουδαῖος in the definition of Tragedy the rendering 'heroic'; the tragic hero is morally superior (potentially) to ordinary modern man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select protagonists with elevated social station or capacity for greater virtue (classification by potentiality) when composing traditional tragedy; consider historical/social context when adapting for modern audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification by potentiality, not actuality
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification should be based on potential (dynamis) rather than realized state (energeia); e.g., a king is classed by capacity for highest virtue even if not actualized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defining characters, genres, or objects, evaluate inherent capacities or types (what something can be) rather than only their present manifestations — this affects character selection and dramatic stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced vs exhausted alternatives in diction (Greek formulae)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Greek formulas ἤτοι---ἤ (balanced alternatives) vs. ἢ---ἤ (exhausted alternatives) differ: balanced alternatives are relative to a standard and include intermediates; exhausted alternatives exclude intermediates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate such oppositions carefully: use 'relatively virtuous or vicious' for balanced alternatives to preserve the inclusion of intermediates; avoid false binary English renderings like 'either virtuous or vicious' when Greek implies relativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sweetening of language (rhythm, harmony, tune; mixture of familiar/unfamiliar)
rubrics_metrics.description: Language is 'sweetened' by restraint (number/metre), rhythm, harmony (tune), and by 'mixture of the familiar with the unfamiliar in diction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In composing verse/prose, use metre and numerical restraint to sweeten parts of the work; purposely mix familiar vocabulary with surprising terms to achieve the Aristotelian 'sweetening' in diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sweetening = restraint; metre as sweetening agent
rubrics_metrics.description: From Rhetoric: 'sweetening = restraint' (περαίνεσθαι); restraining is effected by number (metre).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use formal constraints (metre, rhythm) selectively in parts of a piece to impose restraint that enhances aesthetic pleasure; understand which sections are governed by metre or tune.

rubrics_metrics.name: Esoteric style: precision, economy, and internal system-dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: Esoteric style uses no superfluous words; order is arranged with utmost care; comprehension often requires knowledge of the whole system (the author expects members of his school to understand).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If adopting an esoteric/learned style, be deliberate: every word serves a purpose, syntactic order is significant, and some obscurities may be intentional for a specialist audience; avoid accidental obscurity if not aiming at insiders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate polysemy: using words in multiple senses
rubrics_metrics.description: The author often uses a single word in different senses within the same paragraph or sentence (e.g., θεωρεῖν for 'gaze' and 'use the understanding'; μανθάνειν ambiguously).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit polysemy intentionally to layer meanings, but be aware this can confuse general readers; in translation, mark or disambiguate senses where necessary to preserve argumentative force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translator's care with praxis / energeia / πάθος / πρᾶξις
rubrics_metrics.description: Key Greek terms (πρᾶξις, πάθος, praxis vs. motion vs. energy) carry nuanced philosophical distinctions — e.g., praxis may be 'life', 'career', 'to experience', sometimes 'action'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose English equivalents contextually: sometimes render πρᾶξις as 'experience', 'faring', or 'conduct'; reserve 'action' or 'practice' only where Aristotle's notion of deliberate, purposive activity is meant; annotate choices for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rendering μιμεῖσθαι: prefer 'simulate/feign' over plain 'portray'
rubrics_metrics.description: The English 'simulate' or 'feign' better capture μιμεῖσθαι's technical meaning in this treatise than 'portray'; 'portray' can understate the element of pretense often required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When translating or describing imitation in poetry, use words that convey intentional feigning or simulation where Aristotle implies it; avoid neutral 'portray' when the Greek suggests artful pretense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic pleasure from 'making out' (μανθάνειν ambiguity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's μανθάνειν can mean both 'to receive knowledge' and 'to make out' (to use knowledge); in Poetics the sense intended is closer to 'making out,' which gives pleasure — e.g., solving, recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose works that allow readers to exercise recognition and 'making out' (puzzle-solving, detecting resemblance) to produce intellectual pleasure; be mindful of ambiguous verbs that invite this effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipatory economy: texts may anticipate later points and omit explicit markers
rubrics_metrics.description: In esoteric style clauses anticipate subsequent passages (e.g., anticipation of ὃ 3), and certain words are omitted as superfluous because the following material completes the thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When structuring a complex theoretical or poetic argument, you may rely on anticipatory structure and economy of expression, but ensure overall coherence for intended readers; in translation, consider restoring overt markers if their absence misleads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-familiarity versus invention: exploit but do not depend on prior knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet may profit from audience familiarity with certain names or stories, but invention is permissible (e.g., inventor-names like Antheus); art can use familiar material to advantage without being historically truthful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cultural/reference points to enrich reception while ensuring the invented or altered elements maintain internal plausibility; don't assume all readers share specialist background.
